notes.meaning: Paul left the philosophical city of Athens and walked about fifty miles west to Corinth. Corinth was a wealthy, bustling port city famous across the ancient world for its trade and its deep moral corruption. Paul chose to enter this difficult city because its location offered a wonderful chance to spread the good news in every direction.

In Corinth, Paul met a Jewish man named Aquila and his wife Priscilla, who had recently arrived from Italy. The Roman emperor Claudius had commanded all Jews to leave Rome after rioting broke out in the city. Paul sought this couple out and quickly formed a close and lasting friendship with them.

Paul moved in and worked with Aquila and Priscilla because they shared the same trade of making tents. It was common Jewish custom to teach young men a practical craft so they could always earn an honest living. Paul chose to work with his own hands so he would not be a financial burden to new believers or be accused of preaching for money.

Every Sabbath, Paul went to the local Jewish synagogue to present reasoned arguments from the Scriptures. He spoke with both Jewish listeners and Greek Gentiles who had come to worship the God of Israel. In this way, he worked hard to lead his hearers step by step toward faith in Christ.

When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul felt an even deeper urge to preach the message with full strength. Their arrival and good news refreshed his spirit and allowed him to focus entirely on the ministry. He testified boldly to the Jewish community that Jesus is the Christ, God's promised Savior.

Many of his listeners bitterly fought against his words and spoke insulting, blasphemous things against the message. In response, Paul shook out the dust from his clothing to show he was completely free from blame for their choice. He told them they alone were responsible for their ruin, and he announced that he would now direct his preaching to the Gentiles.

Paul left the synagogue and moved his teaching center next door to the home of a man named Titus Justus. Justus was a God-fearing Gentile who opened his doors so the preaching could go on without interruption. Setting up right beside the synagogue made it easy for any curious or seeking people to walk in and listen.

Despite the opposition, Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord along with his entire household. His decision to follow Jesus made a strong impression across the city. Many other Corinthians who heard the good news also believed and were baptized into Christ.

One night, the Lord Jesus spoke directly to Paul in a vision to lift his spirits during a time of tension and danger. Jesus commanded him not to be afraid and told him to keep speaking out boldly. God's messengers can always take courage knowing that their Lord sees their fears and calls them forward.

The Lord promised Paul His personal presence and pledged that no enemy would be allowed to harm him in Corinth. Jesus also told him that He had many people in that corrupt city waiting to be gathered into the church. This comforting assurance gave Paul the confidence he needed to keep working without fear.

differ.view: God calls them His people because He chose them in eternity, guaranteeing they will certainly come to faith when called.
God calls them His people because He foreknows those who will choose to believe in Christ when the gospel is preached.

notes.meaning: Encouraged by the vision, Paul settled in Corinth for a year and a half. He spent this long season teaching the word of God to ground the new believers firmly in their faith. Patient teaching helps young believers grow strong roots against the sinful pressures around them.

When Gallio became the Roman governor of Achaia, the Jewish leaders joined together to launch an attack against Paul. They seized him and brought him before the governor's official judgment seat in the city square. They hoped the new ruler would take their side and punish Paul as a lawbreaker.

The accusers argued that Paul was urging people to worship God in ways that violated the law. They likely meant Roman law, hoping Gallio would treat Christian preaching as an illegal and harmful religion. In reality, Paul was simply showing how God had kept His ancient promises through Jesus.

Just as Paul got ready to speak in his own defense, Gallio stepped in and addressed the crowd. He told the accusers that if Paul had committed an actual crime or dishonest act, it would be his job as a judge to listen. But he had no interest in ruling on religious complaints.

Gallio saw the matter as nothing more than a religious argument over Jewish words, titles, and internal laws. He instructed the accusers to sort out the disagreement among themselves because he refused to act as a judge over such things. His decision established a helpful boundary between civil law and religious debates.

Gallio then firmly dismissed the entire crowd and drove the accusers away from the judgment seat. He refused to give their charges any further attention or courtroom time. This quick action ended the legal danger facing Paul without the apostle having to say a single word.

The crowd turned its frustration on Sosthenes, the new synagogue leader who had led the charge, and beat him right in front of the judgment seat. Gallio looked the other way and showed no concern for the brawl. Even so, God kept His promise to shield Paul, and Sosthenes himself seems to have later become a Christian brother.

Paul stayed on in Corinth for quite a while before bidding the believers a fond farewell. Before sailing for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, he had his head shaved at the port of Cenchrea to mark the end of a special vow to God. This voluntary act showed his personal thankfulness to the Lord and his ongoing respect for his Jewish heritage.

The travelers crossed the Aegean Sea and reached the great city of Ephesus, where Paul left Priscilla and Aquila. Paul entered the local synagogue and held reasoned discussions about the Scriptures with the Jews. Even during a brief travel stop, he eagerly used the chance to talk about Christ.

The people in the Ephesian synagogue warmly urged Paul to stay longer to teach them. In many other cities the crowds had turned hostile almost right away, but here they welcomed his message. Despite their friendly plea, Paul felt he had to keep moving toward his destination.

Paul said goodbye, explaining that he needed to reach Jerusalem for the coming festival. He promised to return to Ephesus later if God allowed it, and then he set sail. Submitting all our plans to God's will is a healthy reminder that our days are in His hands.

Paul landed at the port of Caesarea, went up to Jerusalem to greet the church, and then headed north to Antioch in Syria. Antioch was the home congregation that had originally sent him on his journey. This safe arrival brought his second missionary journey to a successful close.

After spending some time resting in Antioch, Paul set out on his third missionary journey through Galatia and Phrygia. He visited the young congregations one by one, encouraging the believers and helping them grow in their faith. Faithful ministry involves strengthening existing disciples just as much as reaching new ones.

Meanwhile, a Jewish man named Apollos arrived in Ephesus from the famous educational city of Alexandria in Egypt. He was a gifted, well-spoken man who possessed a deep understanding of the Old Testament Scriptures. God had prepared his mind and voice to become a valuable servant of the church.

Apollos had learned the basic truth about the Lord and spoke with warm, fiery enthusiasm as he taught accurately about Jesus. However, his knowledge was limited because he only understood John the Baptist's message of repentance and hope. Even with partial understanding, he eagerly shared everything he had learned so far.

differ.view: Apollos's knowledge only of John's baptism points to an incomplete spiritual state that needed the baptism of the Holy Spirit.
Apollos was already a true believer whose only lack was fuller factual instruction about Christ's finished work and the Spirit.

notes.meaning: Apollos began speaking boldly in the synagogue, where Priscilla and Aquila heard him preach. Instead of correcting him in public, the couple warmly invited him to their home and explained God's full plan of salvation more clearly. Apollos showed admirable humility by gladly learning from ordinary tentmakers.

When Apollos decided to cross over to Achaia, the Ephesian believers encouraged him and wrote a letter asking the disciples in Corinth to welcome him. After he arrived, his teaching was a huge blessing to those who had come to faith through God's grace. He helped water and tend the spiritual garden that Paul had planted.

In open public debates, Apollos powerfully answered Jewish objections and proved from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. His strong mastery of God's word helped clear away doubts and silenced critics. His successful defense of the truth gave new confidence and joy to the local church.
